title: Rain Shadow Road Trip
description: Plan a drive across an invented mountain range: pick the drier stops, order route legs by expected rainfall using supplied rules, and match landforms to their weather effects.

questions.prompt: Which stop is likeliest to be driest for your picnic?
questions.context: Invented scenario: the north-south Kestrel Range sits inland. Moist air arrives from the west, rises over the range, then sinks on the far side. Use this simplified model.

options.label: Alder Cove, mid-way up the western slope
Pine Flat, just east of the crest
Saltmarsh, a western coastal town at sea level
Ridge Camp, high on the western slope

questions.explanation: Air that has crossed the crest has already shed much of its moisture, so the sheltered eastern side is the rain shadow. Western slope stops sit where air is forced upward.

questions.prompt: Wind direction has flipped. Which stop is likeliest to be driest now?
questions.context: Invented scenario: on the Harrow Range, a steady moist wind blows from the east toward the west. The crest runs north-south. Use this simplified model.

options.label: Westmere, just west of the crest
Dunlow, on the plain east of the range

questions.explanation: The sheltered side is whichever side faces away from the incoming wind. With easterly wind, that is the west, so the rain shadow flips with wind direction.

questions.prompt: Under the simplified model, where would you expect the heaviest rain on this drive?
questions.context: Invented scenario: you drive west to east across the Marlow Range while moist air also moves west to east. The four stops are spaced along the road.

options.label: A flat coastal plain before any climbing
The western slope close to the crest
A basin 80 km downwind of the crest

questions.explanation: Rainfall tends to build as moist air is lifted, so the upper windward slope is wettest in this model. Downwind stops receive progressively drier air.

questions.prompt: Why is the sheltered side of a range often drier?

options.label: Descending air warms, so its moisture is less likely to condense into rain
Mountains create new water vapor on their eastern sides
Sinking air always cools and forms heavy cloud
Rain cannot fall on any land that sits lower than a crest

questions.explanation: After shedding moisture on the way up, air sinks and warms, which keeps remaining vapor from condensing easily. That produces the drier rain-shadow zone.

questions.prompt: Order the four legs from highest to lowest expected annual rainfall.
questions.context: Invented model: base rainfall is 800 mm. Wind blows west to east. Multipliers: windward slope ×2.2, windward coastal plain ×0.9, lee valley ×0.3, far downwind plain ×0.6.

items.label: Eastern valley just beyond the crest
Western slope climbing to the crest
Wide plain far east of the range

questions.explanation: The values work out to 1760 mm on the slope, 720 mm on the coast, 480 mm on the far plain, and 240 mm in the lee valley.

questions.prompt: Wind now arrives from the east. Order these legs from highest to lowest expected rainfall.
questions.context: Invented model: base rainfall is 600 mm. Multipliers: windward slope ×2.0, windward lowland ×1.0, far lee plain ×0.5, lee valley ×0.25. The crest runs north-south.

items.label: Valley just west of the crest

questions.explanation: With easterly wind the values are 1200 mm on the eastern slope, 600 mm on the eastern lowland, 300 mm on the far western plain, and 150 mm in the western valley.

questions.prompt: Match each landform position to its expected weather effect in a rain-shadow model.

left.label: Windward slope facing incoming moist air
Valley just beyond the crest, away from the wind
Coastal ridge facing the incoming sea air
Basin far downwind of the range

right.label: Rising air cools; more rain expected
Sinking air warms; drier conditions expected

questions.explanation: Both windward faces force air upward, boosting rain. Both sheltered positions receive air that has already crossed the range and is drying out.

questions.prompt: Match each change to its likely effect on the rain shadow.
questions.context: Use the simplified model: moist air, one range, and a clear windward and lee side.

left.label: The range erodes into low hills
Wind runs parallel to the range
Air arriving is already very dry

right.label: Former lee side becomes the windward side
Rain shadow weakens as lifting lessens
Neither side has a clear windward or lee contrast
Little rain falls on either side

questions.explanation: A rain shadow depends on wind direction, lift from the range, and available moisture. Changing any of those changes which side is wet or dry.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All ranges, towns and rainfall values here are invented simplified models. Real places vary, so do not treat these figures as local climate data.

title: City-Region-Country Relay
description: Pass real cities to their provinces, estados or states, sort those regions into Canada, Mexico or the United States, then complete city-region-country chains across all three countries.

questions.prompt: Match each city to the province, estado or state where it is located.
questions.explanation: Vancouver is in British Columbia and Halifax in Nova Scotia. Monterrey is in Nuevo León and Oaxaca City in Oaxaca. Austin, Texas is in the United States. Jalisco was a distractor.

questions.prompt: Which of these cities is located in the province of Manitoba?
questions.explanation: Winnipeg is in Manitoba. Halifax is in Nova Scotia, Montreal is in Quebec, and Mérida is in the Mexican estado of Yucatán.

questions.prompt: Guadalajara is a city in which Mexican estado?
questions.explanation: Guadalajara is in Jalisco. Yucatán holds Mérida, Nuevo León holds Monterrey, and Oaxaca holds Oaxaca City.

questions.prompt: Match each region to its country.
questions.explanation: Quebec and Ontario are Canadian provinces; Yucatán and Jalisco are Mexican federal entities. Texas is a state of the United States.

questions.prompt: Which group lists only Mexican federal entities?
questions.explanation: Yucatán, Nuevo León and Oaxaca are all Mexican federal entities. Each other group mixes in a Canadian province.

questions.prompt: Counting its provinces and territories together, how many first-level regions does Canada have?
questions.explanation: Canada has 10 provinces and 3 territories, which makes 13 in total.

questions.prompt: Complete each relay by choosing the missing link in every chain.
questions.explanation: Toronto sits in Ontario, Mérida in Yucatán (in Mexico), and Manitoba (in Canada) contains Winnipeg. Austin is in Texas, in the United States. Each chain runs city, region, country.

questions.prompt: Exactly one relay has every link correct. Which one is it?
questions.explanation: Montreal is in Quebec, which is in Canada. The others break a link: Jalisco is not Monterrey's estado, Halifax is not in Ontario, and British Columbia is Canadian.

sources.label: Government of Canada: regions
INEGI: territorial divisions
City of Austin: official website
Texas State Preservation Board: Texas Capitol, Austin

note: This version covers Canada, Mexico and the United States, with one US city (Austin) and one US state (Texas). Other US states are not covered, and all items have text-only answer choices.

title: The Time-Zone Rendezvous
description: Solve eight clock puzzles using fixed October 18, 2026 UTC offsets: convert meeting times, check availability windows, and sort cities by local clock time.

sections.title: Shared meeting slots
sections.description: Convert times and find windows that work.

sections.title: Clock order
sections.description: Compare local clocks across cities.

questions.prompt: A meeting starts at 9:00 in Vancouver. What does the local clock read in each of these cities at that moment?
questions.context: Fixed offsets for Oct 18, 2026: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Winnipeg UTC-5, Toronto UTC-4, Halifax UTC-3. Use only these offsets, never a live clock.
questions.explanation: Vancouver 9:00 is 16:00 UTC. Adding each offset gives Halifax 13:00, Mexico City 10:00 and Winnipeg 11:00.

questions.prompt: A call starts at 8:00 in Winnipeg. Is each city's local start time inside an 8:00–18:00 window?
questions.context: Same Oct 18, 2026 offsets: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Winnipeg UTC-5, Toronto UTC-4, Halifax UTC-3. All times are on Oct 18.
questions.explanation: Winnipeg 8:00 is 13:00 UTC. That makes Vancouver 6:00, Mexico City 7:00, Toronto 9:00 and Halifax 10:00, so only Toronto and Halifax are inside the window.

questions.prompt: A night call starts at 02:00 on Oct 19 in Halifax. What local date and time is it in each city?
questions.context: Oct 2026 offsets: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Winnipeg UTC-5, Toronto UTC-4, Halifax UTC-3. Watch for the date line between Oct 18 and Oct 19.
questions.explanation: Halifax 02:00 Oct 19 is 05:00 UTC. Vancouver is 22:00 Oct 18, Mexico City 23:00 Oct 18, Winnipeg 00:00 Oct 19, Toronto 01:00 Oct 19.

questions.prompt: Which Vancouver start time gives a one-hour call that fits inside everyone's free window?
questions.context: Free windows in local time on Oct 18, 2026: Vancouver 8:00–12:00, Mexico City 11:00–15:00, Halifax 14:00–18:00. Offsets: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Halifax UTC-3. The call must end by each window's close.
questions.explanation: In UTC the windows are 15:00–19:00, 17:00–21:00 and 17:00–21:00, so all three overlap from 17:00 to 19:00 UTC (10:00–12:00 Vancouver). A one-hour call must start between 10:00 and 11:00 Vancouver, and 10:00 is the only listed option in that range.

questions.prompt: Order these readings by local clock time, from earliest in the day to latest.
questions.context: Each item gives a UTC reading and a city. Oct 18, 2026 offsets: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Winnipeg UTC-5, Toronto UTC-4, Halifax UTC-3. Compare the resulting local clock readings.
questions.explanation: Local readings are Mexico City 8:30, Winnipeg 11:00, Halifax 12:00, Vancouver 13:00 and Toronto 13:30. Sorting those gives the order.

questions.prompt: At 12:00 UTC on Oct 18, match each clue to the city it describes.
questions.context: Offsets for Oct 18, 2026: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Winnipeg UTC-5, Toronto UTC-4, Halifax UTC-3. At 12:00 UTC the clocks read: Vancouver 5:00, and the others follow from their offsets.
questions.explanation: At 12:00 UTC the readings are Vancouver 5:00, Mexico City 6:00, Winnipeg 7:00, Toronto 8:00, Halifax 9:00. Each clue matches exactly one city.

cells.label: Earliest clock reading of the five
Latest clock reading of the five
Exactly one hour ahead of Vancouver
Exactly three hours ahead of Vancouver

questions.prompt: Which city's clock reaches midnight at the start of Oct 19 first? Order the cities from first to last.
questions.context: Oct 18, 2026 offsets: Vancouver UTC-7, Mexico City UTC-6, Winnipeg UTC-5, Toronto UTC-4, Halifax UTC-3. Each city's local midnight happens at a different UTC moment.
questions.explanation: Local midnight Oct 19 falls at 03:00 UTC in Halifax, 04:00 in Toronto, 05:00 in Winnipeg, 06:00 in Mexico City and 07:00 in Vancouver.

questions.prompt: A Halifax friend finishes a call at 23:30 on Oct 18. What are the local date and time in Vancouver?
questions.context: Oct 18, 2026 offsets: Vancouver UTC-7 and Halifax UTC-3. Vancouver is four hours behind Halifax.
questions.explanation: Halifax 23:30 is 02:30 UTC on Oct 19. Subtracting seven hours gives 19:30 on Oct 18 in Vancouver.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
NIST: unit conversion

note: All offsets are fixed assumptions for October 18, 2026, and the availability windows are invented. Nothing uses a live clock, so reason only from the offsets given in each puzzle.

title: Postcard Perspective Puzzle
description: Read tiny invented maps, track which way each window faces, and decide which postcard views are possible and which are contradictions.

sections.title: Pick the Possible View
sections.description: Use position and direction to find views that fit the map.

sections.title: Spot the Impossible Postcard
sections.description: Find the detail that breaks the map.

questions.prompt: Which postcard could have been drawn from the cabin's east-facing window?
questions.context: Invented map: a lake lies directly east of the cabin. A pine ridge lies to the north. A small village lies to the south. Facing east, north is on your left and south is on your right.

options.label: Lake straight ahead, pine ridge at the left edge, village roofs at the right edge
Lake straight ahead, pine ridge at the right edge, village roofs at the left edge
Village straight ahead, pine ridge at the right edge, lake at the left edge
Pine ridge straight ahead, lake at the left edge, village at the right edge

questions.explanation: Facing east puts the lake ahead, north on the left and south on the right. Only the first postcard keeps the ridge left and the village right.

questions.prompt: Standing at the lookout tower in the map's centre and facing west, which zone lies straight ahead?

diagram.title: Top-down map of Saltmarsh Bay (invented)
diagram.description: Schematic map with north at the top. The lookout tower is at the exact centre of the map, not shown as a zone. Fish market sits top-left, boat harbor middle-left, salt flats middle-right, orchard bottom-centre.

questions.explanation: West is the left side of a north-up map. The harbor shares the tower's centre height, while the fish market sits well north of that line.

questions.prompt: Looking north from the hotel balcony, which postcard obeys the occlusion rule?
questions.context: Invented scene. Rule: a feature directly behind a taller building is hidden. Straight north: a 40 m glass tower, with a 15 m museum directly behind it. A 25 m radio mast stands north-east, clear of both. A bay lies north-west.

options.label: Glass tower with museum visible above it, bay at the left
Glass tower in the centre, radio mast to its right, bay at the left
Glass tower in the centre, radio mast to its left, bay at the right
Museum in front of the glass tower, radio mast at the right

questions.explanation: The museum is hidden behind the taller tower. Facing north, the north-east mast appears right and the north-west bay appears left.

questions.prompt: Match each postcard subject to the window direction that could have drawn it.
questions.context: Invented map around a hilltop cabin: a radio mast stands to the north. A pond lies to the east, with a boathouse on its far shore, also east. Apple orchard rows lie to the south. A trailhead sign is to the west.

left.label: Pond with the boathouse behind it

questions.explanation: The pond and boathouse are both east, so two postcards share the east window. The orchard is south and the mast is north.

questions.prompt: Which claimed view through the hotel's north-facing window conflicts with the map?
questions.context: Invented map: the harbor lies only to the south of the hotel. A ski slope rises to the north. A church tower stands north-east. A parking lot lies west.

options.label: Harbor water filling the view straight ahead
Church tower toward the right side
Parking lot toward the left side

questions.explanation: The harbor is south, behind a north-facing window. The slope is ahead, the north-east tower is right, and the west lot is left.

questions.prompt: The postcard is drawn from a ferry deck facing south. Mark each detail as possible or impossible.
questions.context: Invented map: a lighthouse stands to the south. Mountains lie east. A pier lies west. A cliff lies north, behind the deck. Facing south, east is on your left and west is on your right.

cells.label: Lighthouse ahead with the pier at the right edge

questions.explanation: Facing south, the west pier is on the right and the east mountains are on the left. The cliff is north, behind the viewer.

questions.prompt: A postcard from the viewer shows all four features clearly. Which feature would the ridge actually hide?
questions.context: Invented scene: the viewer at the far left faces east. The pine ridge is 60 m tall and the fire tower is 20 m tall, directly behind it. The meadow and pond are ground level and lie beside the ridge's ends.

diagram.title: Top-down sightline map (invented)
diagram.description: North is at the top. The viewer stands at the far left middle, facing east. A narrow tall pine ridge is directly ahead, with the fire tower on the same line behind it. The meadow lies to the north-east and the pond to the south-east, both clear of the ridge.

questions.explanation: The fire tower is on the viewer's line of sight behind a taller ridge. The meadow and pond sit off that line, so both stay visible.

questions.prompt: A postcard claims to be from the museum's south-facing window, showing the fountain left and the arch right. What breaks it?
questions.context: Invented map: the museum sits at the south edge of a square. The fountain is north-west of the museum and the arch is north-east of it.

options.label: The fountain and arch are on swapped sides, but the square is otherwise in view
The square lies north, so a south-facing window looks away from both features
The arch should be drawn taller than the fountain
The fountain should appear farther away than the arch

questions.explanation: Both features are north of the museum, but a south-facing window looks the other way. Swapping sides could not fix a view that points away.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All maps, places and sightline rules are invented for this puzzle. Each scene gives every direction and height you need, so no outside geography knowledge is required.

title: Mexico Beyond the Beach
description: Match inland Mexican cities to their states, check how Mexico is divided, then read invented elevation and drainage maps to sort highlands from lowlands.

questions.prompt: Match each Mexican city to the federal entity (state) where it is located.
questions.explanation: Monterrey is in Nuevo León, Guadalajara in Jalisco, Mérida in Yucatán, and Oaxaca City in Oaxaca. Sonora was the unused distractor.

questions.prompt: How many federal entities does Mexico's territorial division include?
questions.explanation: INEGI describes Mexico as divided into 32 federal entities, which covers the states plus Mexico City.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Mexico City and the State of Mexico is accurate?
questions.explanation: They are separate federal entities. Mexico City is not part of the State of Mexico, despite the similar names.

options.label: Mexico City lies inside the State of Mexico
They are two names for the same entity
Mexico City is not part of the State of Mexico
Mexico City is a town within Oaxaca

questions.prompt: What is the ridge line that separates the two drainage basins called?
questions.context: On an invented valley map, two streams start on opposite sides of one ridge. One stream flows to Laguna Norte, the other to Laguna Sur.
questions.explanation: A divide separates drainage basins. Water on each side of it drains to a different outlet.

questions.prompt: Using the given factor, about how many feet is a 1,500 m mountain pass?
questions.context: Use this fixed assumption: 1 meter = 3.28 feet.
questions.explanation: Multiply 1,500 by 3.28 to get 4,920 feet. Stating the conversion factor keeps the result exact.

questions.prompt: Order these invented routes by average elevation, from highest to lowest.
questions.context: Invented data: Mesa Trail averages 1,900 m, Llano Road 30 m, Cumbre Loop 2,850 m, and Barranca Descent 700 m.
questions.explanation: Sorting by the supplied averages gives Cumbre Loop 2,850, Mesa Trail 1,900, Barranca Descent 700, then Llano Road 30.

questions.prompt: Order these invented water bodies from most upstream to most downstream.
questions.context: Invented map: Manantial Frío feeds Arroyo Alto. Arroyo Alto joins Río Medio. Río Medio empties into Laguna Baja.
questions.explanation: Water follows the stated flow: the spring feeds the creek, the creek joins the river, and the river ends in the lagoon.

questions.prompt: Classify each invented station using the elevation rule given.
questions.context: Invented rule: Highland is 2,000 m or more. Midland is 800 to 1,999 m. Lowland is under 800 m. Stations: Cerro Pino 2,650 m, Valle Seco 1,200 m, Playa Norte 15 m, Mesa Larga 2,100 m.
questions.explanation: Cerro Pino and Mesa Larga are at or above 2,000 m, Valle Seco falls in the middle band, and Playa Norte is far below 800 m.

title: Borderless Watersheds
description: Follow rivers across an invented map from tributary to bay to ocean, then test divides, nested basins, inland lakes and alternate place names.

sections.title: Rivers to outlets
sections.description: Trace each river to its receiving water and ocean.

sections.title: Divides and nesting
sections.description: Use watershed boundaries to sort drainage.

sections.title: Missing links and edge cases
sections.description: Complete chains and handle inland lakes and alias names.

questions.prompt: Connect each river to the receiving water where its flow first reaches a sea, bay or gulf.
questions.context: Invented map. Alder River flows into Marrow Bay. Brindle River flows into Tern Gulf. Calder River flows into Selkie Sound. Dune Creek joins Alder River, which carries all of its water onward.
questions.explanation: Tributaries share the outlet of the river they join. Dune Creek feeds Alder River, so both end up in Marrow Bay.

questions.prompt: Connect each receiving water to the ocean it belongs to, treating the bay or sea as a separate layer.
questions.context: Invented map, real ocean names. Marrow Bay opens to the Pacific Ocean. Cormorant Sea is an arm of the Pacific Ocean. Tern Gulf opens to the Atlantic Ocean. Selkie Sound connects through Hale Strait to the Arctic Ocean.
questions.explanation: Several bays and seas can open into the same ocean. Marrow Bay and Cormorant Sea both belong to the Pacific here.

questions.prompt: Water leaves Dune Creek and travels through every link downstream. Which ocean does it finally reach?
questions.context: Use the invented map: Dune Creek joins Alder River. Alder River enters Marrow Bay. Marrow Bay opens to the Pacific Ocean.

options.label: Marrow Bay, because a bay counts as an ocean

questions.explanation: Follow the chain creek, river, bay, ocean. Marrow Bay is only the intermediate receiving water; the ocean it opens to is the Pacific.

questions.prompt: Two raindrops land 20 metres apart on opposite sides of Ridge Hollow Divide. What happens to them?
questions.context: Invented map. Ridge Hollow Divide separates the Alder basin from the Brindle basin. Alder basin water drains to Marrow Bay. Brindle basin water drains to Tern Gulf. A divide separates drainage basins.

options.label: They reach different receiving waters, Marrow Bay and Tern Gulf
Both reach Marrow Bay because they started close together
Both reach Tern Gulf because the divide is a ridge
They meet on the divide and stay there

questions.explanation: A divide sends water down opposite sides into different basins. Closeness at the start does not matter; the side of the divide decides the outlet.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Dune Creek basin and the Alder basin is correct?
questions.context: Invented map. The Dune Creek basin sits entirely inside the Alder basin. Dune Creek joins Alder River. Alder River enters Marrow Bay. Larger basins can contain smaller ones.

options.label: Dune Creek's basin is nested in the Alder basin and shares its Marrow Bay outlet
The two basins are separated by a divide and have different outlets
The Alder basin lies inside the Dune Creek basin
Dune Creek's water must reach a different ocean from Alder River

questions.explanation: A smaller basin can sit inside a larger one. Its water leaves through the larger basin's outlet, so both share Marrow Bay.

questions.prompt: Fill each missing link so the river-to-water-to-ocean chain is complete.
questions.context: Invented map. Pike River enters Gull Gulf, which opens to the Atlantic. Quill River enters Selkie Sound, which connects to the Arctic. Moss River enters Cormorant Sea, an arm of the Pacific. Tern Gulf also opens to the Atlantic.
questions.explanation: Each chain must follow the stated connections. Match the river's entry point, then the ocean that water opens to.

questions.prompt: Which description of Ash River's drainage fits the supplied facts?
questions.context: Invented map. Ash River flows into Lake Osprey. Lake Osprey has no outlet stream and loses water by evaporation. In this quiz, a water path reaches an ocean only if flowing surface links connect to it.

options.label: It drains to an inland lake with no surface path to any ocean
It reaches the Pacific Ocean through Marrow Bay
It reaches the Atlantic Ocean through Tern Gulf
It reaches the Arctic Ocean through Hale Strait

questions.explanation: A basin whose water ends in a lake without an outlet is inland-draining. Under the stated convention it has no ocean outlet.

questions.prompt: Local signs call Selkie Sound 'Sealskin Bay'. A river enters Sealskin Bay. Which ocean does its water reach?
questions.context: Invented map. Naming policy: aliases refer to the same water body and never change drainage. Sealskin Bay is another name for Selkie Sound, which connects through Hale Strait to the Arctic Ocean.

options.label: Pacific Ocean, because the name changed
Atlantic Ocean, because bays drain east
No ocean, because the alias is not on the main map

questions.explanation: Two names for one water body share the same connections. The alias does not alter the path, so the river still reaches the Arctic.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
USGS: watersheds

note: The rivers, bays and sounds here are invented and all facts are supplied in each question. Only the ocean names and general watershed ideas (outlets, divides, nested basins) are real.

title: One River, Three Clues
description: Solve four invented river puzzles by narrowing four candidates with three clues each, choose the clue that settles two bonus puzzles, then check basic watershed ideas.

questions.prompt: Using all three clues, which of the four candidate rivers is the one described?
questions.context: Invented rivers. Alder: 420 km, flows north, boundary river, ends in a lake. Birch: 420 km, flows south, boundary river, ends in a sea. Cedar: 310 km, flows south, boundary river, ends in a sea. Dunn: 420 km, flows south, inside one country, ends in a sea. Clues: 1) It forms part of an international boundary. 2) It is longer than 400 km. 3) It empties into a sea.
questions.explanation: Clue 1 removes Dunn, clue 2 removes Cedar, and clue 3 removes Alder. Only Birch satisfies all three.

questions.prompt: Which candidate river fits every one of the three clues?
questions.context: Invented rivers. Eska: 600 km, highland source, delta mouth, crosses two countries. Fenn: 600 km, plateau source, delta mouth, crosses two countries. Garro: 600 km, highland source, estuary mouth, crosses two countries. Holm: 250 km, highland source, delta mouth, one country. Clues: 1) It crosses two countries. 2) Its source is in highlands. 3) It ends in a delta.
questions.explanation: Clue 1 eliminates Holm, clue 2 eliminates Fenn, and clue 3 eliminates Garro. Eska is the only match.

questions.prompt: Apply the clues in order. Which river remains after the third clue?
questions.context: Invented rivers. Nessa: 800 km, flows west, 3 dams. Orla: 500 km, flows east, 3 dams. Morro: 600 km, flows east, 1 dam. Linna: 800 km, flows east, 3 dams. Clues: 1) It is longer than 550 km. 2) It flows east. 3) It has at least two dams.
questions.explanation: Length keeps Nessa, Morro and Linna. Flowing east leaves Morro and Linna. Only Linna has at least two dams.

questions.prompt: Convert the first clue, then use all clues. Which river is described?
questions.context: Use 1 km = 0.62 miles. Invented rivers. Pella: 300 km, boundary river, ends in a lake. Quill: 300 km, boundary river, ends in a sea. Rusk: 120 km, boundary river, ends in a lake. Sable: 260 km, inside one country, ends in a lake. Clues: 1) It is at least 150 miles long. 2) It forms an international boundary. 3) It ends in a lake.
questions.explanation: Pella and Quill are about 186 miles, Sable about 161, and Rusk about 74. Boundary removes Sable; the lake ending removes Quill.

questions.prompt: Which extra clue would leave exactly one candidate river?
questions.context: Invented rivers. Tarn: boundary, 500 km, flows north, ends in a sea. Ulla: boundary, 500 km, flows south, ends in a sea. Vane: boundary, 350 km, flows north, ends in a lake. Wick: not a boundary, 500 km, flows north, ends in a sea. Known clues: it forms a boundary and is longer than 400 km.
questions.explanation: The known clues leave Tarn and Ulla. Only Tarn flows north; the other three clues still fit both rivers.

questions.prompt: Which extra clue uniquely identifies the river among the candidates?
questions.context: Invented rivers. Xan: highland source, 3 bridges, flows north, delta. Yore: highland source, 3 bridges, flows south, delta. Zell: highland source, 5 bridges, flows south, estuary. Ames: lowland source, 5 bridges, flows south, delta. Known clue: its source is in highlands.
questions.explanation: Highlands leaves Xan, Yore and Zell. Only Zell has an estuary; the other clues each leave at least two rivers.

questions.prompt: Match each creek to the outlet where its water finally leaves the system.
questions.context: Invented map. Ash and Bell Creeks join the Upper Fork, which flows into Marl River. Cove Creek flows straight into Marl River. Ember Creek joins Dale Creek, and Dale Creek empties into Dale Bay, separated from Marl River by a ridge divide.
questions.explanation: Streams in the same drainage basin share a common outlet. The divide keeps Dale and Ember water out of the Marl River system.

questions.prompt: Mark each watershed statement as true or false.

cells.label: A divide separates one drainage basin from a neighboring basin.
A divide is the point where a basin's water leaves.
A larger basin can contain a smaller basin.
A watershed drains toward a common outlet.

questions.explanation: A watershed drains to a shared outlet, and divides separate basins rather than serving as outlets. Smaller basins can nest inside larger ones.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
USGS: watersheds
NIST: unit conversion

note: All rivers, creeks and their lengths in the clue puzzles are invented, and every needed fact is given in each question. Clues appear together, so there is no reveal penalty. Only the watershed ideas come from a real reference.

title: The Missing Transit Stop
description: Solve six clue grids about invented transit lines, finding dropped stops and rebuilding stop orders, then finish with a clue-ordering task and a distance puzzle.

sections.title: Find the dropped stop
sections.description: Compare plans, logs and rider clues.

sections.title: Rebuild the order
sections.description: Place stops in positions using clues.

questions.prompt: Compare the planned stop list with the rider's log, then answer both parts.
questions.context: Invented Lakeshore Line plan, in order: Mill, Lakefront, Junction, Stadium, Airport. A rider's log of stops where the train actually called: Mill, Lakefront, Stadium, Airport.
questions.explanation: Junction appears in the plan but not in the log, so it was dropped. With it gone, Stadium now directly follows Lakefront.

questions.prompt: Use the timetable and the rider's timestamps to find the missing stop and the long hop.
questions.context: Invented Teal Line timetable, minutes after departure: Reed 0, Quay 3, Dome 6, Fern 9, Gate 12, Peak 15. A rider's log shows calls at Reed 0, Quay 3, Dome 6, Gate 12 and Peak 15.
questions.explanation: Gate came 6 minutes after Dome instead of 3, so the 9-minute stop, Fern, was skipped. The 6-minute hop started at Dome.

cells.label: The 6-minute hop in the log started at

questions.prompt: Deduce where the unannounced transfer stop sat in the planned line.
questions.context: Invented Harbor Line has five planned stops. A rider boarded at the first planned stop and heard every call: Lakefront, Stadium, Museum, Airport. Exactly one planned stop was dropped. The posted plan numbers Stadium as stop 3.
questions.explanation: The rider boarded at stop 1 and heard Lakefront first, so Lakefront is stop 1. Stadium is planned stop 3 but was the second call, so the dropped stop is planned stop 2, between Lakefront and Stadium.

cells.label: Its position in the planned order

questions.prompt: Fill each position on the invented Amber Line using all four clues.
questions.context: Stops: Harbor, Library, Mill, Park. Clues: Harbor is first. Park is neither first nor last. Mill comes after Library. Library is directly before Park.
questions.explanation: Harbor is first. Library directly before Park leaves Library-Park-Mill or Mill-Library-Park; Mill after Library rules out the second, giving Harbor, Library, Park, Mill.

questions.prompt: Rebuild the five-stop invented Violet Line from the rider clues.
questions.context: Stops: Depot, Lakefront, Transfer, Stadium, Zoo. Clues: the transfer comes after Lakefront and before Stadium. Zoo is directly after Stadium. Depot is the last stop.
questions.explanation: Depot is last. Lakefront, Transfer and Stadium must stay in that order, and Zoo directly follows Stadium, so the line runs Lakefront, Transfer, Stadium, Zoo, Depot.

questions.prompt: Place the stops of the invented Coral Line using counting clues.
questions.context: Stops: Aster, Bridge, Cove, Dock, Elm. Clues: Elm is the last stop. Bridge is exactly two stops before Elm. Dock is directly before Bridge. Aster comes before Cove.
questions.explanation: Elm is 5th, so Bridge is 3rd and Dock 2nd. Aster and Cove fill 1st and 4th, and Aster must come before Cove.

questions.prompt: Combine three rider reports to order the four stops of the invented Sun Line.
questions.context: Rider 1 says Hub comes before Zoo. Rider 2 says Quay comes before Stadium. Rider 3 says Stadium comes before Hub. All reports are about the same direction of travel.
questions.explanation: Quay precedes Stadium, Stadium precedes Hub, and Hub precedes Zoo. Chaining the three reports gives one order: Quay, Stadium, Hub, Zoo.

questions.prompt: Which planned stop was skipped on this invented Mill Line trip?
questions.context: Planned hops in km: Mill to Park 2, Park to Dune 3, Dune to Rail 1, Rail to Port 4. A rider heard Mill, then a stop 5 km from Mill, then Rail 1 km later, then Port.
questions.explanation: Dune sits 2 + 3 = 5 km from Mill, so it is the stop the rider heard. Park, between Mill and Dune, was skipped.

title: Seven-Hour Layover Lab
description: Eight quick layover choices, from scenarios to rankings and pairs, place you on two descriptive preference scales: rest versus activity, and familiar surroundings versus sensory variety.

dimensions.description: Whether a long wait feels best spent recharging in place or moving around.
Whether you settle into known comforts or seek new sights, sounds and tastes while waiting.

questions.prompt: Your connection is delayed seven hours. What is your first move?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. Napping or chatting leans toward rest and comfort, while heading out or circling the terminal leans toward activity.

options.label: Find a quiet seat near the gate and nap
Walk to a nearby neighborhood to look around
Text a friend and settle in for a long chat
Pace the terminal on a loop of places you know

questions.prompt: Hour two arrives. Which way of passing it sounds most natural?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. Resting or rereading a favorite book leans toward rest; brisk laps lean toward activity. A new snack counter adds sensory variety, while a familiar book or route keeps things familiar.

options.label: Recline with an eye mask and rest
Stretch your legs with brisk laps of the concourse
Sample something unfamiliar at a local snack counter
Reread a favorite book in your usual way

questions.prompt: Your gate changes to the far end of the terminal. What do you do?
questions.explanation: A gate change shows how you treat disruption: keeping a setup, treating it as a chance to explore, or using it as a reason to move.

options.label: Settle at the new gate and recreate your cozy setup
Wander over slowly and look at everything new on the way
Walk quickly and use the distance as exercise
Ride the moving walkway and watch a show you have never seen

questions.prompt: You have one hour of free Wi-Fi left. How do you use it?
questions.explanation: This round separates how active you want to be from how much novelty you want. Both axes can point different ways.

options.label: Message familiar people you have been meaning to catch up with
Start a podcast on a topic completely new to you
Work through a checklist of small tasks you know well
Go hunting for a terminal exhibit or live performance

questions.prompt: Rank these ways to spend the final delayed hour, from most to least appealing.
questions.explanation: Items near the top count most toward your two preference scales. None of them is a better way to travel.

items.label: Play a favorite playlist by the gate
Try a food you have never had

questions.prompt: Across a long wait, how much do you want each hour to feel different from the last?
questions.explanation: The left end means a steady, repeating routine; the right end means a fresh sight, sound or taste every hour.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the delay to the kind of activity you would choose for it.
questions.explanation: Several parts can share one activity. Where you place nap, stroll, chat and tasting reveals how your energy and curiosity shift across a long delay.

questions.prompt: Which pair option is more tempting right now?
questions.explanation: This pair splits the two axes: one option is still but novel, the other active but familiar. Your pick shows which pull is stronger.

options.label: Sit by a window and watch unfamiliar planes and people
Walk your usual loop past favorite shop corridors

title: Twin Cities Across the Line
description: Pair invented border towns from clues and schematic diagrams, then match real Canadian and Mexican cities to their provinces and states.

sections.title: Reading the border map
sections.description: Invented towns and schematic diagrams.

sections.title: Real country duos
sections.description: Cities and their provinces or states.

questions.prompt: Match each invented border town to the partner town facing it across the line.
questions.context: Invented region. Each town faces exactly one partner. Northvale's bridge lights are visible from Saltmere. Pinecrest and Tollgate share a river ferry. Eastport faces Marrow Bay across a strait. Dunmore's partner is the remaining town.
questions.explanation: Three clues name partners directly, so the only town left unpaired, Cedarholt, must face Dunmore.

questions.prompt: In this invented twin-town diagram, which zone is the river boundary shared by both towns?

diagram.title: Harbor Town and Ridge Town (invented schematic)
diagram.description: Schematic rectangles, not a real map. Harbor Town sits on the north bank at top left. A wide river channel runs across the middle. Ridge Town sits on the south bank at bottom right. A dry hill park sits at bottom left.

questions.explanation: The channel lies between the two town banks, so it is the feature both towns face and share.

questions.prompt: Rain falling on which zone would divide toward two different drainage basins?
questions.context: A divide separates drainage basins, and each watershed drains to a common outlet.

diagram.title: Two valleys and a lake (schematic)
diagram.description: Schematic rectangles, not a real map. A western basin and an eastern basin sit side by side, separated by a narrow central ridge line. A lake strip along the bottom is where both basins drain.

questions.explanation: The ridge between the two basins is the divide, so water on its two sides flows into different basins.

questions.prompt: Which invented twin pair has the largest combined population?
questions.context: Invented populations in thousands. Northvale 40, Saltmere 55. Pinecrest 70, Tollgate 18. Eastport 52, Marrow Bay 47. Dunmore 30, Cedarholt 60.
questions.explanation: The totals are 95, 88, 99 and 90 thousand, so Eastport and Marrow Bay lead even though Pinecrest is the biggest single town.

questions.prompt: Match each Canadian city to the province where it lies.
questions.explanation: Vancouver is in British Columbia, Montreal in Quebec, Halifax in Nova Scotia and Winnipeg in Manitoba. Ontario is left over for Toronto.

questions.prompt: Match each Mexican city to the federal entity where it lies.
questions.explanation: Monterrey is in Nuevo León, Guadalajara in Jalisco, Mérida in Yucatán and Oaxaca City in Oaxaca. Sonora matches none of these cities.

questions.prompt: How many provinces and territories does Canada have in total?
questions.explanation: Canada has 10 provinces and 3 territories, which makes 13 in total.

questions.prompt: How many federal entities does Mexico have?
questions.explanation: Mexico is divided into 32 federal entities, which are its states plus Mexico City.

title: The Altitude Ladder
description: Climb a three-rung ladder of invented survey stations: sort elevations into bands, link mean temperatures to profiles, then complete full point-to-band-to-profile chains.

questions.prompt: Using this activity's bands, which band holds Mesa Alta, a station at 2,200 metres?
questions.context: Bands used here: Lowland under 500 m; Foothill 500–1,499 m; Highland 1,500–2,599 m; High Sierra 2,600 m and above. These are this activity's labels, not universal climate rules.
questions.explanation: 2,200 m is at least 1,500 and below 2,600, so it falls in the Highland band.

questions.prompt: Sort these invented stations from lowest to highest elevation. Convert feet to metres first.
questions.context: Use 1 metre = 3.281 feet. Some stations list metres, others feet. Costa Verde 40 m; Lomas 2,950 ft; Mesa Alta 2,200 m; Pico Nube 10,330 ft.
questions.explanation: Converted, Lomas is about 899 m and Pico Nube about 3,148 m. The order is Costa Verde, Lomas, Mesa Alta, Pico Nube.

questions.prompt: Match each invented station to its elevation band.
questions.context: Bands: Lowland under 500 m; Foothill 500–1,499 m; Highland 1,500–2,599 m; High Sierra 2,600 m and above. More than one station can share a band.
questions.explanation: Valle Seco (1,720 m) and Mesa Alta (2,200 m) both sit in the Highland band; the others each fall in a different band.

questions.prompt: Lomas has a mean annual temperature of 21.4°C. Which profile does it get?
questions.context: Profiles by mean annual temperature: Warm 22°C or more; Mild 16–21.9°C; Cool 10–15.9°C; Cold under 10°C. These are this activity's definitions.
questions.explanation: 21.4°C is below the 22°C Warm threshold but at least 16°C, so Lomas is Mild.

questions.prompt: Match each station's mean annual temperature to its profile.
questions.context: Warm 22°C or more; Mild 16–21.9°C; Cool 10–15.9°C; Cold under 10°C. Stations can share a profile.
questions.explanation: Valle Seco (17.6°C) and Lomas (21.4°C) are both Mild. Mesa Alta at 15.2°C is Cool, and Pico Nube at 7.8°C is Cold.

questions.prompt: Complete the chains for Cantera and Nieblas by choosing each band and profile.
questions.context: Cantera: 1,490 m, 19.8°C. Nieblas: 2,640 m, 9.6°C. Bands: Lowland under 500 m; Foothill 500–1,499; Highland 1,500–2,599; High Sierra 2,600+. Profiles: Warm 22+°C; Mild 16–21.9; Cool 10–15.9; Cold under 10.
questions.explanation: Cantera at 1,490 m just misses Highland, so it is Foothill and Mild. Nieblas passes 2,600 m and averages under 10°C: High Sierra and Cold.

questions.prompt: Connect each station to every band and profile label that applies to it.
questions.context: Sol Llano: 380 m, 24.9°C. Tierra Fresca: 1,980 m, 13.4°C. Brisa: 560 m, 21.9°C. Bands: Lowland under 500 m; Foothill 500–1,499; Highland 1,500–2,599. Profiles: Warm 22+°C; Mild 16–21.9; Cool 10–15.9.
questions.explanation: Each station gets one band and one profile. Brisa is Foothill and Mild because 21.9°C is just under the Warm line.

questions.prompt: An invented station sits at 2,610 m with a mean of 9.9°C. Which full chain is correct?
questions.context: Bands: Highland 1,500–2,599 m; High Sierra 2,600 m and above. Profiles: Cool 10–15.9°C; Cold under 10°C.
questions.explanation: 2,610 m reaches the 2,600 m line for High Sierra, and 9.9°C is under 10°C, so the chain is High Sierra and Cold.

title: Long June Days or Short December Ones?
description: Compare June and December daylight for Canadian and Mexican cities using supplied rounded latitudes and a stated daylight rule, then apply that rule in ordering, matching and grid tasks.

sections.title: Pairs on a fixed date
sections.description: Pick the city with the longer daylight.

sections.title: Season and latitude
sections.description: Use latitude to match patterns.

questions.prompt: On the June solstice, which city gets longer daylight?
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed for this quiz: Whitehorse, Yukon is 60.7°N. Mérida, in the Mexican state of Yucatán, is 21.0°N.
questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere's summer, higher latitudes tilt further toward the Sun, so Whitehorse's day is much longer than Mérida's.

questions.prompt: On the June solstice, which city has more hours between sunrise and sunset?
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed: Halifax, Nova Scotia is 44.6°N. Oaxaca City, in the Mexican state of Oaxaca, is 17.1°N.
questions.explanation: Both are north of the equator in summer, and the one farther north has the longer June day. Halifax wins by a clear margin.

options.label: They are equal at the solstice
Neither, since both are in the same time zone

questions.prompt: Which city enjoys longer daylight on the June solstice?
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed: Vancouver, British Columbia is 49.3°N. Monterrey, in the Mexican state of Nuevo León, is 25.7°N.
questions.explanation: Vancouver sits much farther north, so its summer-solstice day is longer. Latitude is the deciding clue, not nearness to the coast.

questions.prompt: Now try the December solstice: which city gets longer daylight?
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed: Winnipeg, Manitoba is 49.9°N. Guadalajara, in the Mexican state of Jalisco, is 20.7°N.
questions.explanation: In northern winter the pattern flips. Higher northern latitudes get shorter days, so lower-latitude Guadalajara has more daylight than Winnipeg.

options.label: Winnipeg, because it is farther from the equator

questions.prompt: Order these cities by June solstice daylight, longest first.
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed: Whitehorse 60.7°N, Winnipeg 49.9°N, Toronto 43.7°N, Mérida 21.0°N.
questions.explanation: In June, daylight lengthens steadily as northern latitude increases. The order simply follows latitude from 60.7°N down to 21.0°N.

questions.prompt: Match each place and date to its daylight pattern.
questions.context: Compare each day with a 12-hour day. At 60°N the June day is far longer than 12 hours and the December day far shorter. At 21°N the swing is small.
questions.explanation: Near 60°N the seasonal swing is huge. Near 21°N it is gentle, with June slightly over 12 hours and December slightly under.

questions.prompt: For each city and date, is daylight longer or shorter than 12 hours?
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed: Whitehorse 60.7°N, Mérida 21.0°N, Halifax 44.6°N, Oaxaca City 17.1°N. Solstice dates only.
questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, June solstice days exceed 12 hours and December solstice days fall short of 12, at every one of these latitudes.

questions.prompt: A traveler wants the biggest difference between June and December day lengths. Which city should they pick?
questions.context: Rounded latitudes assumed: Mérida 21.0°N, Halifax 44.6°N, Winnipeg 49.9°N, Whitehorse 60.7°N.
questions.explanation: The seasonal swing in day length grows with distance from the equator. Whitehorse, the farthest north, has the largest June-to-December difference.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
Government of Canada: regions
INEGI: territorial divisions

note: Latitudes are rounded values assumed for this quiz. Rule used throughout: in the Northern Hemisphere, days are longer than 12 hours at the June solstice and shorter than 12 hours at the December solstice, and the difference grows with latitude. None of these cities is far enough north for true midnight sun. Only the qualitative pattern is tested, not exact daylight hours, and no live data is used.

title: Named Winds and Lake Snow: An Invented Map
description: Match four invented named winds to their regions, work out what causes each, then read weather-station records and a causal chain to identify the event behind them.

questions.prompt: Using the map notes, match each local weather phenomenon to the region where it would occur.
questions.context: Invented map: westerly winds (blowing from west to east) prevail. Cards: Karrow is warm, dry gusts on the downwind side of a mountain crest. Dunmere is hot, dry air flowing seaward from a high inland basin. Marrow snow is heavy snow just downwind of a large unfrozen lake in cold air. Tolvana is strong gusts funnelled through a narrow gap. Notes: the Tessel Range runs north-south. The Corvane Coast lies west of the high Ombrel Basin. Lake Ombre is a large lake with a western and an eastern shore. Halden Pass is a narrow gap between two ranges.

right.label: Eastern foothills of the Tessel Range

questions.explanation: Westerlies cross the Tessel crest and descend on its east side. Dunmere drains seaward from the basin to the coast. Lake snow falls on the downwind (eastern) shore. Gaps funnel wind.

questions.prompt: Why is a Karrow wind on the lee side of a range typically warm and dry?

options.label: Air sinks down the slope, is compressed and warms, after losing moisture earlier
It picks up heat from an unfrozen lake
It is squeezed through a narrow pass
It comes straight off a warm ocean current

questions.explanation: Descending air is compressed and warms, and it has often already dropped moisture on the windward side, so it arrives warm and dry.

questions.prompt: A Dunmere wind blows from the Ombrel Basin toward the sea. What pressure pattern drives that direction?

options.label: Lower pressure inland and higher pressure over the sea
Higher pressure over the inland basin and lower pressure near the coast
Equal pressure everywhere, with wind caused only by the Moon
Higher pressure over the lake and lower pressure over the pass

questions.explanation: Air flows from higher toward lower pressure, so high pressure inland and lower pressure near the coast pushes air seaward.

questions.prompt: Why does Marrow snow fall on the downwind shore rather than evenly around the lake?

options.label: Snow is blown in from the ocean as salt crystals
Warm air sinks over the shore and freezes the lake
Cold air gains heat and moisture crossing the lake, then rises and cools over land
The lake itself freezes and drops snow

questions.explanation: Cold air crossing warmer open water picks up moisture and heat, then lifts and cools on reaching land, releasing snow downwind.

questions.prompt: Why can Tolvana gusts be much stronger inside Halden Pass than on the open plains beside it?

options.label: The pass is always warmer than the plains
Air is forced through a narrow gap and speeds up when pressure differs across it
Mountains create new air that adds to the wind
Lake water pulls the air faster

questions.explanation: A narrow gap channels airflow, and with a pressure difference across it the air accelerates, producing stronger gusts than in open terrain.

questions.prompt: Match each invented station record to the weather event it documents.

cells.label: Foothill station, 14 Jan: temperature up 12 C in two hours, humidity 80% to 25%, west gusts over the crest
Coast station, 3 Oct: 38 C at 9 pm, humidity 9%, wind from the inland basin
Lakeshore station, 2 Dec: air -8 C, lake water 6 C, 25 cm snow in 12 hours with wind off the lake

questions.explanation: A fast winter warm-up with falling humidity fits Karrow; late-night heat and dryness from inland fits Dunmere; snow with cold air over warmer lake water fits Marrow.

questions.prompt: Put the lake-snow steps in the order they must happen.

items.label: Cold air moves out over the open lake
Air gains heat and moisture from the water
Air rises over land and cools into clouds
Snow falls on the downwind shore

questions.explanation: Each step depends on the one before: air must cross the lake, be warmed and moistened, then lift and cool before snow can fall.

questions.prompt: A Tolvana gust is recorded at 90 km/h. Using 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, what is that in m/s?
questions.explanation: Divide km/h by 3.6: 90 / 3.6 = 25 m/s. Multiplying instead gives the wrong 324.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
NIST: unit conversion

note: The winds, regions and station records here are invented teaching cases, not real places or forecasts. They illustrate general patterns such as downslope warming, offshore flow, lake-effect snow and gap winds.

title: Same Distance, Different Numbers
description: Convert distances between kilometres, miles, metres and feet using supplied factors, then check map scales and elevation labels in eight short tasks.

sections.title: Sign pairs
sections.description: Match signs that describe the same distance in different units.

sections.title: Scale checks
sections.description: Catch misleading scales and mislabeled distances or heights.

questions.prompt: A trail sign says 10 kilometres. Which second sign describes about the same distance?
questions.context: Use 1 km = 0.621 miles. Round to the nearest whole mile.
questions.explanation: 10 × 0.621 = 6.21, which rounds to 6 miles. Kilometres are shorter than miles, so the mile number must be smaller.

questions.prompt: Match each sign in miles to the kilometre sign showing about the same distance.
questions.context: Use 1 mile = 1.609 km. Round each result to the nearest whole kilometre. One kilometre sign is a decoy.

questions.prompt: Pick the feet sign matching each metre sign on three viewpoint boards.
questions.context: Use 1 m = 3.28 ft. Round each result to the nearest 10 ft.
questions.explanation: Multiply metres by 3.28: 328, 1,476 and 6,560 feet. Rounded to 10 ft, these become 330, 1,480 and 6,560.

questions.prompt: Order these four signs from the shortest distance to the longest.
questions.context: Use 1 mile = 1.609 km and 1,000 m = 1 km.
questions.explanation: In kilometres: 1.5 miles ≈ 2.41, 2,500 m = 2.5, 4 km = 4, and 3 miles ≈ 4.83. Converting everything to one unit makes the order clear.

questions.prompt: On a reduced copy, two towns are 3 cm apart. What is their real distance?
questions.context: The original map's bar says 1 cm = 5 km. The copy was shrunk to half its length and width, and the bar was not redrawn.
questions.explanation: After halving, 1 cm on the copy stands for 10 km. So 3 cm is 30 km. Using the old bar would wrongly give 15 km.

questions.prompt: A hiking map has a ratio scale of 1:50,000. A path measures 4 cm. How long is it really?
questions.explanation: 4 cm × 50,000 = 200,000 cm. Dividing by 100 gives 2,000 m, which is 2 km.

questions.prompt: A pass sign shows 6,000 ft. Which metre label is correctly converted and rounded?
questions.context: Use 1 ft = 0.3048 m. Round to the nearest 10 m.
questions.explanation: 6,000 × 0.3048 = 1,828.8 m, which rounds to 1,830 m. A foot is shorter than a metre, so the metre number is smaller.

questions.prompt: How many miles long is the 6 cm trail drawn on this map?
questions.context: The scale bar shows 0, 5 and 10 miles, and the whole bar is 4 cm long. The trail is 6 cm on the same map.
questions.explanation: 4 cm equals 10 miles, so 1 cm is 2.5 miles. Then 6 cm × 2.5 = 15 miles.

description: Eight quick scenarios and habit pairs place your own preferences on two scales: Landmarks to Street Geometry, and Asking Directions to Self-Checking.

sections.title: Lost in a new place
sections.description: Pick what you would actually do.

sections.title: Natural habits
sections.description: Choose the habit that feels more like you.

Whether you tend to confirm your way by talking to people or by checking maps, signs and notes yourself.

questions.prompt: You are lost in a new neighborhood with no clear plan. What do you do first?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. This shows which cue you reach for first when your bearings slip.

options.label: Head toward the tallest building I can see
Follow the street grid and count blocks
Ask the nearest person for directions
Stop and study my own map or notes

questions.prompt: When you give a friend directions, which style sounds more like you?
questions.explanation: Route descriptions built on places or on turns and distances show which cue feels natural to explain.
questions.highLabel: Go two blocks east, then north

questions.prompt: You leave a train station by an unfamiliar exit. Which first move feels most natural?
questions.explanation: Each choice is a valid habit. Together they show whether you anchor on places, layout, people or your own checking.

options.label: Find a distinctive building and orient from it
Work out which way the streets run
Ask station staff which exit I need
Read the posted area map carefully

questions.prompt: Rank these first moves in a big park, from most natural to least natural.

items.label: Aim for a visible tower or statue
Trace the straight paths on the posted map

Note path names and junctions as I walk

questions.explanation: Several situations can share one approach. Your pattern across them shows where your habits are consistent.

left.label: Finding a cafe in a new town
Finding a meeting room in a large building

right.label: Check a map on my own

questions.explanation: Both are common ways to store a route: as a chain of places or as a set of directions and blocks.

options.label: A chain of memorable places along the way
A sequence of blocks, turns and compass directions

questions.explanation: This pair looks at confirmation style only. It says nothing about how well you navigate.

options.label: Check with a local or shop worker
Re-check street signs and my own notes

title: Landscape Knowledge, Landscape Taste
description: Answer four landform and drainage questions for an accuracy score, then make four taste choices that place your own preferences on two scales: Intimate scenes to Panoramic vistas, and Linger and observe to Roam and explore.

sections.title: Landform Knowledge
sections.description: Four scored tasks about drainage, erosion and deposition.

sections.title: Landscape Taste
sections.description: Four unscored preference tasks with no right answers.

dimensions.description: Whether you lean toward tucked-away, enclosed landscapes or wide, open horizons.
Whether you prefer to settle in and watch a landscape or cover ground moving through it.

questions.prompt: Rain falling on the west side of a ridge flows to River A; rain on the east side flows to River B. What is the ridge?
questions.explanation: A divide separates drainage basins, sending runoff toward different outlets depending on which side it lands on.

questions.prompt: Which process best explains the Karu Notch in these field notes?
questions.context: Invented field notes for the Karu Notch: a steep-walled, narrow cut with a flowing stream on its floor. The rock shows no ice scratches, and no sand dunes or wind-piled ridges are nearby.
questions.explanation: Running water cutting downward through rock fits a narrow notch with a stream at the bottom. Ice scratches or dunes would point elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Match each process clue to the landform it builds.
questions.context: Invented teaching glossary: a sea cliff is a rock face worn back by waves; a delta forms where a river slows and drops sediment into standing water; a dune is a wind-piled sand ridge; a canyon is a deep valley cut by flowing water.
questions.explanation: Each landform is named for its main process: waves for sea cliffs, slowing water for deltas, wind for dunes, and downward cutting for canyons.

left.label: Waves undercut rock at the shore
A river slows and drops silt into a lake
Wind piles loose sand into ridges
Flowing water cuts steadily down through rock

questions.prompt: Order the journey of one raindrop through an invented watershed, from first to last.
questions.context: Invented Selmo watershed: a raindrop lands on a ridge-side slope, and all runoff eventually leaves by the watershed's single common outlet at the sea.
questions.explanation: Runoff gathers in small streams, joins larger rivers, and finally leaves through the common outlet shared by the whole watershed.

items.label: The river reaches the common outlet at the sea
Runoff collects in a small stream
Rain falls on a ridge-side slope
The stream joins a larger river

questions.prompt: You have one free morning. Which landscape visit sounds best?

Sitting by a wide bay to watch the light change
Resting in a quiet sheltered cove

title: Fair Midpoint Meetup
description: Work through invented travel-time tables together to find the venue with the shortest longest journey, then discuss which compromise your group would choose.

questions.prompt: Which venue gives the smallest longest journey for any of the three friends?
questions.context: Invented cities. Travel times in minutes for Asha, Bo and Cleo. Lakeside: 90, 60, 120. Hillcross: 80, 100, 70. Portgate: 60, 110, 95. Millford: 105, 95, 90.
questions.explanation: Compare each venue's largest time: Lakeside 120, Portgate 110, Millford 105, Hillcross 100. Hillcross has the smallest maximum.

questions.prompt: A different group cares about combined travel time instead. Which venue has the smallest total across all three friends?
questions.context: Invented venues, minutes for three friends. Ridge: 40, 50, 150. Harbor: 80, 85, 90. Quarry: 60, 70, 100. Junction: 55, 75, 120.

questions.prompt: Fill in the longest journey for each venue, then pick the minimax venue.
questions.context: Invented towns, minutes for Dee, Eli and Fay. Northfold: 45, 80, 60. Eastmere: 70, 65, 55. Southwick: 90, 50, 75.

cells.label: Venue with the smallest longest journey

questions.prompt: Order the venues from smallest to largest longest journey.
questions.context: Invented venues, minutes for Gil, Hana and Ivo. Pinecourt: 50, 95, 70. Orchard: 110, 40, 65. Fenwick: 75, 75, 75. Quay Street: 85, 60, 80.

questions.context: Invented venues, minutes for three friends. Cedar Point: 50, 60, 55. Dunmore: 70, 45, 40. Elmgate: 30, 80, 60. Fairhaven: 90, 60, 70.
questions.explanation: Cedar Point is 60 minus 50, Dunmore 70 minus 40, Elmgate 80 minus 30 and Fairhaven 90 minus 60. Two venues share a 30-minute gap.

questions.prompt: Using 60 minutes per hour, which venue has the smallest longest journey?

questions.prompt: Connect each friend to every venue they can reach in 60 minutes or less.

options.label: Alder, to cap anyone's longest trip
Alternate between them on different meetups
Ask the person with the longest trip to choose

title: Detour Diary: Prairie to Pacific
description: Work through a fictional prairie-to-coast drive with route, ferry, fuel and landform puzzles solved from the data given. Your answer to the first question decides which final question appears.

questions.prompt: Which choice gets you to Saltport sooner?
questions.context: Invented trip: you leave Wheatmark on the prairie for Saltport on the coast. The Fern Gap pass road takes 9 hours of driving, but fog closes it for the next 5 hours. The inland highway is open and takes 13 hours.

options.label: Wait 5 hours, then take the pass road

questions.explanation: Waiting costs 5 + 9 = 14 hours in total, while the inland highway takes 13. The longer road wins by one hour.

questions.prompt: What is the ridge line that separates those two drainage basins called?
questions.context: On the invented map, rain falling on Fern Gap's west slopes runs to Salt Sound, while rain on its east slopes runs to Lake Marrow. The summit ridge keeps the two catchments apart.
questions.explanation: A divide separates drainage basins. Each basin drains to its own common outlet, here Salt Sound on one side and Lake Marrow on the other.

questions.prompt: Order the ferry-route stops so every rule is respected.
questions.context: Invented rules: you must refuel at Cedar Bend and cross Hollow Bridge before climbing Mist Ridge. The ferry at Pine Landing comes after the climb, and arriving in Saltport comes after the ferry. Refuel and bridge order is not fixed.
questions.explanation: Both early stops must precede the climb, the climb precedes the ferry, and the ferry precedes arrival. Either order of refuel and bridge works.

questions.prompt: Match each invented landform to the travel challenge it creates.
questions.context: Tallgrass Plain: flat ground for 300 km. Fern Gap: a pass at 1,900 m between peaks. Salt Sound: a sea inlet 6 km wide with no bridge. Marrow Narrows: a 1 km strait with no road across. Mist Ridge: a steep slope above the tree line.
questions.explanation: Flat land suits long straight driving, high passes and steep slopes bring climbs and weather, and wide water with no crossing needs a ferry or bridge.

questions.prompt: At what time would you land at Saltport on the earliest ferry you can board?
questions.context: On the invented ferry route, Pine Landing ferries leave at 10:30, 13:30 and 16:30. Boarding closes 20 minutes before departure, and the crossing takes 2 hours 15 minutes. You reach the landing at 12:50.
questions.explanation: The 13:30 sailing stops boarding at 13:10, so 12:50 is in time. Adding 2 hours 15 minutes gives a 15:45 landing.

questions.prompt: Connect each route to every intermediate stop it passes through.
questions.context: Invented routes. Pass road: Wheatmark, Fern Gap, Saltport. Inland highway: Wheatmark, Cedar Bend, Dry Mesa, Saltport. Ferry route: Wheatmark, Cedar Bend, Hollow Bridge, Mist Ridge, Pine Landing, Saltport.
questions.explanation: Cedar Bend is shared by the inland and ferry routes. Fern Gap belongs only to the pass road, and the other stops each belong to one route.

questions.prompt: Which choice lets you reach Saltport from Dry Mesa without a detour?
questions.context: You took the inland highway. Your car's range is 300 km and the tank was full at Cedar Bend, 140 km back. Saltport is 175 km ahead. Dry Mesa has the only fuel station on this stretch, and no road links it to Fern Gap.

options.label: Refuel at Dry Mesa, then continue
Return to Cedar Bend to refuel
Cut over to the Fern Gap pass road

questions.explanation: You have 300 − 140 = 160 km of range left, which is less than 175 km. Dry Mesa is the fuel stop on your way, and no road reaches Fern Gap.

questions.prompt: What time do you reach Saltport on the pass road?
questions.context: You waited. The fog cleared and you left Wheatmark at 11:00. The pass road takes 9 hours of driving, and you add one 30-minute rest stop on the way.
questions.explanation: 11:00 plus 9 hours of driving is 20:00, and the 30-minute rest stop makes it 20:30. Fog on the high pass is what created the wait.

title: Layered Place Names: An Invented Gazetteer
description: Read invented gazetteer entries and archive snippets to sort place names into language layers, then check a few real city and region links.

questions.prompt: Using the glossary, match each place name to the language layer its main word comes from.
questions.context: Invented glossary. Tavari (an invented Indigenous language): tava = lake, orin = ridge. French: rivière = river. Spanish: sierra = mountain range. English: stone = rock, hill = rise of land.
questions.explanation: Each name is built from a glossary word: rivière is French, sierra is Spanish, stone and hill are English, and tava and orin are Tavari.

questions.prompt: Sort each place into the origin group its ledger entry documents. Several places can share a group.
questions.context: Invented ledger. Mirren Landing: named for surveyor Ada Mirren. Kolu Falls: 'kolu' is Tavari for falls. Teshwa Creek: 'teshwa' is Tavari for cold water. Cedar Bluff: named for cedars growing on the bluff.
questions.explanation: Kolu and Teshwa both come from Tavari words, Mirren honors a person, and Cedar Bluff describes what grows there. Origin groups can hold several places.

questions.prompt: Order these four names for one invented harbor from earliest to latest first written record.
questions.context: Invented archive for a fictional harbor. Each label shows the year its name first appears in a surviving written record.
questions.explanation: By record year the order is 1712, 1744, 1781, 1823. An early written record shows when a name was documented, not necessarily when it began.

questions.prompt: Which claim do these invented records actually support?
questions.context: Fictional harbor archive. An 1840 trader's diary writes 'Walami' for the harbor, noting how local Tavari speakers said it. An 1902 map reads 'Port Valmy'. A 1950 map reads 'Puerto Balmi'.

options.label: A written form 'Walami' predates both maps shown.
The records prove Walami is the only origin of Valmy.
The 1950 map preserves the oldest spelling.
The diary shows the harbor had no earlier name.

questions.explanation: The 1840 diary is older than both maps. The records do not prove a single origin or rule out earlier names.

questions.prompt: A map project wants current community usage. Which entry do these invented records support?
questions.context: Fictional lake. An 1870 survey writes 'Tavalone'. A 2019 list from an invented Tavari community language office gives 'Tava Lun' as the lake's current spelling.

options.label: Show 'Tavalone' as the only correct name.
Show 'Tava Lun' and note 'Tavalone' as a historical spelling.
Show 'Tavalone' because older records always win.

questions.explanation: The 2019 community list documents current usage, while the 1870 survey is useful history. Older does not automatically mean more correct.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the name 'Belmar' is supported by both snippets?
questions.context: Invented records. An 1790 ship's log says Belmar comes from Spanish words meaning beautiful sea. An 1830 Tavari word list gives a similar-sounding word meaning salt flat. Neither source mentions the other.

options.label: The log is right because it is earlier.
The word list is right because it is local.
Two documented explanations exist and these records do not settle which is correct.
The name has no documented origin.

questions.explanation: Both sources document an origin, and the snippets give no way to choose between them. Layered names can have disputed or overlapping origins.

questions.prompt: Match each city to the Canadian province or Mexican state where it lies.
questions.explanation: Halifax is in Nova Scotia, Winnipeg in Manitoba, Monterrey in Nuevo León and Mérida in Yucatán.

questions.prompt: Which of these cities is in the Canadian province of Quebec?
questions.explanation: Montréal is in Quebec. Vancouver is in British Columbia, Toronto is in Ontario, and Oaxaca City is in the Mexican state of Oaxaca.

title: Seen From Orbit: Why It Looks That Way
description: Read eight satellite-style scenes, given as original diagrams and text descriptions, work out what caused each pattern, then match patterns to land use and drainage. Score out of 8 with every pattern explained.

sections.title: Choose the cause
sections.description: Four orbit views, each with a supplied field guide.

sections.title: Patterns and land use
sections.description: Match patterns, read scale, order images and trace drainage.

questions.prompt: Which cause best explains the pattern in this invented orbit card?
questions.context: Invented field guide: a sprinkler arm turning around a fixed hub waters a round field. Impact basins have raised rims and no hub. Volcanic vents sit along cracks, with dark rock around them. Card: eight green circles in two rows on tan dry land. Each has a pale center dot and one thin line from dot to edge.
questions.explanation: The center hub and single radial line match a turning sprinkler arm. Craters would have raised rims and no hub, and vents would follow cracks in dark rock.

questions.prompt: Rain on which strip would split, flowing toward streams on both sides? Select that zone.
questions.context: Schematic top-down diagram, not a photo. Three vertical strips show ground height: the outer strips are low valleys, each with a stream. The middle strip is the highest ground.

diagram.title: Three-strip elevation schematic
diagram.description: Left strip: low valley with a stream. Middle strip: the highest ridge line. Right strip: low valley with a stream.

questions.explanation: A drainage divide is high ground that separates neighboring drainage basins. Rain on the ridge splits and flows down into whichever side it falls toward.

questions.prompt: Which cause fits this card of branching lines?
questions.context: Card: thin dark lines start as many short twigs near the top. They join into thicker lines, then one wide line exits at a single point on the bottom edge. Field guide: planted rows stay parallel, and street grids cross at right angles.

options.label: A stream network draining to one outlet

questions.explanation: Small channels merging downhill into larger ones that reach one outlet is how a watershed drains. Rows and street grids would stay parallel or cross at right angles.

questions.prompt: Where was the sun when this invented card was taken? Select the zone where the sun must be.
questions.context: Schematic top-down diagram, not a photo. Shadows fall directly away from the sun. North is up and east is right. Every tall tower on a flat plain casts a long shadow pointing west, toward the left edge of the card.

diagram.title: Tower shadow and sun-direction schematic
diagram.description: A square card with north at the top and east on the right. A tower stands at the center, and its long shadow points to the left (west). Four labeled zones surround it: a west zone on the left edge, an east zone on the right edge, a north zone along the top, and an overhead zone in the middle around the tower. Choose the zone where the sun is.

options.label: To the west of the towers
To the east of the towers
To the north of the towers

questions.explanation: Shadows point left, which is west, so the sun is the opposite way, to the east. An overhead sun would give almost no shadow.

questions.prompt: Match each orbit pattern to the land use it shows. Some land uses repeat.
questions.context: Invented key. Housing: tiny roofs 10–20 m wide along streets. Cropland: huge single-tone rectangles without roofs. Harbor: long straight quay with stacked boxes beside deep water.

left.label: Thousands of tiny pale squares along curved streets
Colored boxes stacked in rows beside a straight quay
Tiny pale squares in tight rows on dead-end lanes

questions.explanation: Small roofs on streets mean housing, so two patterns share that target. Roofless one-tone rectangles are fields, and stacked boxes by a quay indicate a harbor.

questions.prompt: Using the stated scale, choose the real size of each feature.
questions.context: Scale for this invented card: 1 pixel equals 10 meters.
questions.explanation: Multiply pixels by 10 m: 40 gives 400 m, 3 gives 30 m, and 120 gives 1,200 m. Check zeros carefully when converting scale.

questions.prompt: Order these four views of one invented farm circle from earliest to latest in a single growing season.
questions.context: Invented rules: a circle is tilled before sowing, sprouts appear after sowing, sprouts grow into a dense crop, and harvest leaves pale stubble.
questions.explanation: Tilling comes first, then sprouts, then the dense crop, and stubble only appears after harvest. Each view must follow the one that causes it.

questions.prompt: Rain falls in Creek Basin C. Which basins does that rain count as part of?
questions.context: Invented map: Creek Basin C lies entirely inside River Basin R. River Basin R lies entirely inside Sea Basin S.

options.label: R and S only, not C

questions.explanation: Larger drainage basins can contain smaller ones. Rain landing in C is in C, in the larger R around it, and in the still larger S.
