title: Read the Climate Chart
description: Read invented monthly temperature and rainfall tables, then name each climate pattern and match it to a kind of place. Every chart comes with its full data in text.

sections.title: Name the climate pattern
sections.description: Four charts, four climate shapes.

sections.title: Match to a kind of place
sections.description: Use chart shapes to place stations.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the shape of Station A's chart?

options.label: Mild wet winters and a warm, dry summer
Warm and wet in every month
Below freezing for most of the year

questions.explanation: Rain is highest in the winter months and nearly vanishes from June to August, while temperatures never drop below 9°C. That is a wet-winter, dry-summer shape.

questions.prompt: Using the rules in the options, which label fits Station B?

options.label: Subarctic-style: a long, very cold winter but some months above 10°C

questions.explanation: June, July and August average above 10°C, which rules out the polar rule. The extreme winter lows and light rain match the subarctic rule.

questions.prompt: Tap the block of months holding the greatest total rainfall for Station C.
questions.context: Invented Station C rain (mm), Jan to Dec: 5, 5, 10, 30, 120, 300, 380, 350, 220, 60, 15, 5. The diagram splits the year into four three-month blocks.

diagram.title: Station C rainfall, four quarter-year blocks
diagram.description: Schematic with the year running left to right in four equal blocks: Jan to Mar, Apr to Jun, Jul to Sep, Oct to Dec. Bar heights follow the monthly rain figures given above.

questions.explanation: July to September adds up to 380 + 350 + 220 = 950 mm, far above April to June at 450 mm. This single-season rain peak is the monsoon-style shape.

questions.prompt: Using the rules in the options, which label fits Station D?
questions.context: Invented Station D, Jan to Dec. Rain (mm): 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4. Mean temperature (°C): 14, 16, 20, 25, 30, 34, 36, 35, 32, 26, 19, 14.

options.label: Hot-desert-style: under 250 mm of rain a year and very hot summers
Mediterranean-style: at least one winter month over 60 mm

questions.explanation: The twelve rainfall values total 26 mm and July reaches 36°C. Only the hot-desert rule fits, since no month reaches 60 mm, 150 mm or drops below -10°C.

questions.prompt: Match each chart summary to the kind of place that could produce it. Some places fit more than one chart.

left.label: Chart 1: 26–28°C all year, 200–300 mm of rain every month
Chart 2: 28–35°C, never more than 5 mm of rain in a month
Chart 3: -30°C to 8°C, under 40 mm of rain in any month
Chart 4: 30–38°C, 1–6 mm of rain in each month

questions.explanation: Constant heat with heavy rain suits a rainforest lowland, and constant heat with almost no rain suits a hot desert. Never exceeding 8°C points to polar tundra.

questions.prompt: For each rain chart, choose when the rain peaks.
questions.context: Invented monthly rain (mm), Jan to Dec. Each cell lists one station's figures.
questions.explanation: Look for where the tallest values cluster. Stations E and H peak mid-year, F peaks around the year's turn, and G stays within 70 to 80 mm in every month.

questions.prompt: Order the stations from smallest to largest yearly temperature range.
questions.context: Yearly range means warmest monthly mean minus coolest monthly mean. Invented stations: J warmest 28°C, coolest 24°C. K warmest 20°C, coolest -10°C. L warmest 30°C, coolest 12°C. M warmest 24°C, coolest 9°C.
questions.explanation: The ranges are J 4°C, M 15°C, L 18°C and K 30°C. A small range suggests steady seasons, while a large one suggests a strong winter-summer swing.

questions.prompt: Tap the quadrant of the map where Station N belongs.
questions.context: Invented Station N has an annual mean temperature of 3°C and 1,400 mm of rain a year. On this map, warm means an annual mean above 15°C, and wet means more than 1,000 mm a year.

diagram.title: Temperature and rainfall quadrant map
diagram.description: Schematic grid. Left to right runs from cold to warm annual temperature. Top to bottom runs from wet to dry annual rainfall. Four quadrants are marked.

questions.explanation: 3°C is below the 15°C warm threshold, and 1,400 mm is above the 1,000 mm wet threshold. That places Station N in the cold, wet quadrant at top left.

title: Hear the Landscape
description: Decode short original tone sequences as terrain profiles using a fixed pitch-to-elevation legend, then match, order and classify invented routes by what you hear.

sections.title: Listen and Read
sections.description: Four tone sequences, each with a written transcript.

sections.title: Route Reading
sections.description: Use the same legend on written pitch lists.

questions.prompt: Each tone is one trail stop, in order. Which elevation profile does this sequence describe?
questions.context: Legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. So 300 Hz is 100 m and 700 Hz is 500 m. Higher pitch means higher ground.
questions.transcript: Three evenly spaced tones: 300 Hz, then 500 Hz, then 700 Hz. Each is higher than the last.

options.label: Climbs steadily from 100 m to 500 m
Drops steadily from 500 m to 100 m
Rises to 500 m, then falls back to 100 m

questions.explanation: Subtracting 200 gives 100 m, 300 m and 500 m. Each stop is higher than the last, so the route climbs the whole way.

questions.prompt: The last stop sits lower than the earlier level stretch. How far below that plateau is it?
questions.context: Same legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. Tones are stops along an invented ridge walk.
questions.transcript: Three identical 600 Hz tones, then a final lower 300 Hz tone.
questions.explanation: The plateau is 600 − 200 = 400 m. The final stop is 300 − 200 = 100 m, so the drop is 300 m.

questions.prompt: Four stops alternate between two pitches. Which landform pattern do they trace?
questions.context: Same legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. Stops are in walking order along an invented trail.
questions.transcript: Four tones alternating low and high: 400 Hz, 800 Hz, 400 Hz, 800 Hz.

options.label: Two 600 m highs separated by a 200 m low
One long climb ending at 600 m
A single 600 m peak with gentle slopes

questions.explanation: The tones are 200 m, 600 m, 200 m, 600 m. That is high, low, high with a dip between two equal summits.

questions.prompt: Stops are 2 km apart along a straight descent. What is the average drop per kilometre?
questions.context: Same legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. Consecutive stops are exactly 2 km apart on this invented path.
questions.transcript: Four falling tones in equal 200 Hz steps: 900 Hz, 700 Hz, 500 Hz, 300 Hz.
questions.explanation: Each 200 Hz step is a 200 m drop over 2 km. That is 100 m per kilometre; the total fall is 600 m over 6 km.

questions.prompt: A guide plays the pitches below. Which invented route profile, in stop order, matches them?
questions.context: Legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. Pitches heard in order: 300 Hz, 600 Hz, 600 Hz, 300 Hz.
questions.explanation: Converting gives 100, 400, 400, 100 m: up to a level plateau and back down. The other options reorder those same heights.

questions.prompt: Each invented stop has a pitch. Order the stops from lowest ground to highest ground.
questions.context: Legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. Harbor Gate plays 350 Hz, Mill Bend plays 650 Hz, Cloud Pass plays 950 Hz, and Reed Lake plays 500 Hz.
questions.explanation: The elevations are Harbor Gate 150 m, Reed Lake 300 m, Mill Bend 450 m and Cloud Pass 750 m, so that is the low-to-high order.

questions.prompt: Match each pitch to the elevation band its ground falls in. Some bands fit more than one pitch.
questions.context: Legend: elevation in metres = frequency in Hz minus 200. Bands are exclusive ranges for this puzzle.
questions.explanation: The pitches give 50 m, 250 m, 350 m and 650 m. The middle two both fall in the 200 to 400 m band.

questions.prompt: Read each leg of the invented route between consecutive pitches. Is each leg a climb, level, or a descent?
questions.context: Legend: higher pitch means higher ground. Pitches heard in order: 300 Hz, 500 Hz, 500 Hz, 400 Hz, 700 Hz.
questions.explanation: Compare each pitch with the one before it: higher is a climb, equal is level, lower is a descent. The route rises, flattens, dips, then climbs again.

title: Passenger Seat Rules
description: Choose between road-trip rules and rank your own stopping and passenger duties to see where you land on two descriptive travel scales.

sections.title: Rule pairs
sections.description: Pick the rule you would rather ride with.

sections.title: Rankings and dial
sections.description: Prioritize your own stops and seat duties.

dimensions.description: Whether you prefer to pause for views and detours or keep the trip moving toward the destination.
Whether you naturally take on route-tracking jobs or mood-setting jobs from the passenger seat.

questions.prompt: On a long drive, would you rather stop at every viewpoint or keep going until dinner?
questions.explanation: This pair shows how much you trade progress for views. There is no right answer; it only shapes your Scenic Stops versus Steady Mileage lean.

questions.prompt: The route is clear. Would you rather arrive an hour early or find a surprise stop along the way?
questions.explanation: Early arrival rewards steady driving, while a surprise stop rewards flexibility. Both are valid trip styles, and this choice only moves your pace lean.

questions.prompt: Which passenger job would you happily claim for the whole trip?

options.label: Watch the map and call out turns
Run the playlist, snacks and stories

questions.prompt: The driver looks tired. Which kind of help would you offer first?
questions.explanation: Calling out exits supports steady progress and navigation, while games and stories favor atmosphere and pauses. Either help is reasonable; this simply records your instinct.

options.label: Read upcoming exits and lane changes
Start a game and suggest a break

questions.prompt: During a quiet stretch, would you rather track landmarks on the route or start a car game?
questions.explanation: Tracking landmarks leans toward navigation duties, while starting a game leans toward atmosphere duties. The choice reflects your default seat habit, not skill.

questions.prompt: Rank these stops from the one you would most want to the one you would least want.
questions.explanation: Your order shows which kinds of stops you value. Stops with views or local flavor lean scenic, while quick fuel or an early arrival lean steady mileage.

items.label: Pull over at a hillside viewpoint
Quick fuel stop, then back on the road
Long lunch at a local café
Skip extras to reach the hotel early

questions.prompt: Rank these passenger duties from the one you would most want to the one you would least want.
questions.explanation: Map and distance jobs lean toward navigation duties, while playlist and photo jobs lean toward atmosphere duties. Your ranking creates the second half of your card.

items.label: Read the map and plan turns

questions.prompt: Set the dial for your ideal day of driving, from stopping often to rolling steadily.

title: Itinerary Sanity Check
description: Repair invented day plans by checking travel-time tables for clock clashes, then ordering stops to cut backtracking.

sections.title: Spot the clash
sections.description: Check times against opening hours and departures.

sections.title: Cut the backtracking
sections.description: Reorder stops so the route makes sense.

questions.prompt: Plan A is below. What goes wrong with it?
questions.context: Invented plan. Leave Hotel 08:00. Hotel to Harbor Market is 25 minutes; stay 60 minutes. Market to Clock Tower is 35 minutes. The Clock Tower tour starts at 09:30 and admits no latecomers.

options.label: It reaches the Clock Tower at 10:00, after the 09:30 tour start
It reaches the Market before leaving the Hotel
The Market stay is too short to be useful
It reaches the Clock Tower at 09:00, too early

questions.explanation: 08:00 plus 25 minutes gives 08:25 at the Market. Staying 60 minutes means leaving at 09:25, and 35 more minutes arrives at 10:00.

questions.prompt: By how many minutes does Plan B miss the café's last seating?
questions.context: Invented plan. Lighthouse visit runs 11:00 to 11:50. Lighthouse to Cove Café takes 40 minutes. The café's last seating is at 12:20.
questions.explanation: Leaving at 11:50 and travelling 40 minutes arrives at 12:30. The last seating is 12:20, so the plan is 10 minutes late.

questions.prompt: Check each leg of Plan C. Does it work, or is there a clock clash?

cells.label: Cable car ends 09:45; 30 minutes to Old Fort; the Fort opens at 10:00
Fort visit ends 11:15; 25 minutes to the Pier; the boat leaves at 11:30
Boat returns 12:00; 15-minute walk to the Bakery; the Bakery closes at 12:30

questions.explanation: The Fort leg arrives at 10:15, after opening. The Pier leg arrives at 11:40, after the boat left. The Bakery leg arrives at 12:15, before closing.

questions.prompt: How many minutes of cross-town travel does Plan D contain?
questions.context: Invented plan. Breakfast in the North, lunch in the South, park gate in the North, dinner in the South, in that order. Each North-South crossing takes 40 minutes; travel within an area is negligible.
questions.explanation: The plan goes North to South, South to North, then North to South again. That is three crossings of 40 minutes, or 120 minutes.

questions.prompt: Order the Island Day stops so that every rule holds. Any valid order counts.
questions.context: Invented rules: the Ticket Office must come before the Ferry. The Bell Tower, beside the Ticket Office, must come before the Ferry. The Ferry comes before Island Garden. Harbor Lunch comes after Island Garden.
questions.explanation: Ticket Office and Bell Tower can swap places, but both precede the Ferry. After that the chain is fixed: Ferry, Island Garden, Harbor Lunch.

questions.prompt: Order these stops to cross town only once. Any order that meets every rule counts.
questions.context: Invented plan. Observatory and Café are in the North; Aquarium and Night Market are in the South. Both North stops come before either South stop. The Aquarium comes before the Night Market.
questions.explanation: Finishing both North stops first avoids a second crossing. The Aquarium then precedes the Night Market, leaving only the North pair free to swap.

questions.prompt: Which visiting order covers all three stops with the least travel time, with no return trip?
questions.context: Invented road. Travel time equals the gap between positions, in minutes from the Hotel: Old Town 10, Quarry 30, Lake 45. The Hotel is at 0, and the plan starts there.
questions.explanation: Moving steadily outward costs 45 minutes. The other orders total 85, 100 and 60 minutes because they double back along the road.

questions.prompt: Match each flawed plan snippet to the repair that fixes it.

left.label: Museum opens 10:00, but the plan arrives at 09:40
South café, then North gallery, then South garden
Boat leaves 14:00; a 60-minute gift shop stop causes arrival at 14:10
Two North stops split by a South stop

right.label: Move the stop to a later slot

questions.explanation: Early arrival needs a later slot. Zigzag routes need grouping by area. Missing a departure by 10 minutes means trimming the stop before it.

title: Flat Map, Round World
description: Read four schematic map diagrams to spot which property a projection distorts, then compare four globe routes using supplied angles and distances.

sections.title: Projection diagrams
sections.description: Work out what each flat drawing keeps true and what it bends.

sections.title: Globe routes
sections.description: Use supplied measurements to find the shorter path on a sphere.

questions.prompt: Using the legend, tap the drawing that best supports a fair comparison of land areas.
questions.context: Legend: an equal-area drawing gives equally sized tiles the same drawn area everywhere. Each map below covers a globe with tiles of identical true size. Tile sizes are described in each label.
questions.explanation: Only Map P draws identical true tiles at identical size, so area comparisons stay fair there. The other maps enlarge tiles in some places, which exaggerates apparent land area.

diagram.title: Four schematic maps with tile sizes
diagram.description: Four original rectangles, each a simplified map of a globe covered in tiles of equal true size. Labels state how tile areas appear in each drawing.

zones.label: Map P: all tiles drawn the same size
Map Q: tiles grow larger toward the top edge
Map R: tiles near the side edges drawn twice as large
Map S: tiles near the centre drawn twice as large

options.label: Map P: all tiles drawn the same size
Map Q: tiles grow larger toward the top edge
Map R: tiles near the side edges drawn twice as large
Map S: tiles near the centre drawn twice as large

questions.prompt: Which lake is truly larger, the northern one or the equatorial one?
questions.context: On one drawing, areas in the northern band are enlarged 4 times, and the equatorial band is not enlarged. Same scale: the northern lake measures 20 cm² on the page, and the equatorial lake measures 10 cm².
questions.explanation: Dividing the northern lake's drawn area by its enlargement factor gives 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm² of true-scale area. The equatorial lake's 10 cm² is therefore larger.

questions.prompt: For each map, choose the property that the drawing distorts.
questions.context: Each description gives one effect while the other properties stay faithful.
questions.explanation: Stretched outlines show shape distortion, mismatched sizes show area, unequal spacing for equal separations shows distance, and a changed bearing angle shows direction.

cells.label: Map X: a round lake of the same area is drawn as a long thin oval
Map Y: two lakes of equal true size, one drawn three times larger
Map Z: two town pairs equally far apart on the globe are drawn 2 cm and 5 cm apart
Map W: a true 45° bearing between towns is drawn at 70°

questions.prompt: Tap the band where horizontal distances are drawn at true scale.
questions.context: A stretch factor of 1.0 means a drawn horizontal length equals true scale. Larger numbers mean horizontal lengths are drawn longer than they should be.
questions.explanation: Only the band with factor 1.0 draws horizontal distances at true scale. Bands with factors above 1.0 stretch distances, so measuring there overstates the real separation.

diagram.title: Map divided into four horizontal bands
diagram.description: An original schematic map split into four stacked bands, each labelled with its horizontal stretch factor.

questions.prompt: Which pair of cities is closer along the globe?
questions.context: Invented cities on a sphere. A flat map draws Alder–Brook as 8 cm and Alder–Cedar as 9 cm. Globe great-circle angles: Alder–Brook is 74°, Alder–Cedar is 58°.
questions.explanation: On a sphere of one size, a smaller great-circle angle means a shorter path. Alder–Cedar at 58° beats Alder–Brook at 74°, even though the flat map suggests otherwise.

questions.prompt: Order these routes from shortest to longest on the same globe.
questions.context: All four routes are great-circle arcs on one invented sphere, so a larger central angle means a longer route.
questions.explanation: Sorting by central angle gives 41°, 76°, 93°, then 118°. Because the globe is the same for every route, angle alone decides the ranking.

questions.prompt: Using the rounded route measurements, which route is shorter and by how much?
questions.context: On invented Miniworld, 1° of great-circle arc is 100 km, and the equator is 36,000 km around. Two towns lie on one parallel where 1° of longitude spans 60 km. The straight-looking parallel route covers 50° of longitude. The great-circle route between them spans about 29.4° of arc, rounded to one decimal for this calculation.
questions.explanation: Using the supplied rounded measurements, the parallel route is 50 × 60 = 3,000 km. The great-circle route is 29.4 × 100 = 2,940 km, approximately 60 km shorter.

questions.prompt: For each trip, match the comparison result between the direct arc and the waypoint route.
questions.context: Trip 1: direct 48° versus 25° plus 26° via a waypoint off the direct path. Trip 2: direct 70° versus 35° plus 35° via a waypoint on the direct great circle. Trip 3: direct 90° versus 60° plus 45° via a waypoint off the path.
questions.explanation: Trips 1 and 3 have waypoint totals of 51° and 105°, longer than direct. Trip 2's waypoint lies on the direct arc, so both routes total 70°.

title: Fog Island Contour Navigation
description: Navigate original Fog Island using contour interval interpolation, relative horizontal spacing for slope (fixed linear profile, same units), and an explicit toy-game fog threshold. Schematic 2D rectangular zone diagrams only; all data in text. Contour concept paraphrased from public USGS resources.

questions.prompt: On Fog Island the contour interval is 10 m. Between the 40 m and 50 m contours a point is halfway. What is the interpolated elevation?
questions.context: Original: linear interpolation assumed between adjacent contours. Contours connect equal elevation points (paraphrased public definition).
questions.explanation: Halfway between 40 and 50 is 45 m under linear interpolation.

questions.prompt: Match horizontal spacing to relative slope on the schematic.
questions.context: Original toy: closer contours (smaller horizontal spacing) mean steeper slope. Wider spacing gentler. Fog threshold: spacing < 5 units → high fog risk (steep). For this toy schematic only: spacing up to 2 units is Very steep; greater than 2 and less than 5 is Steep; 5 through 10 inclusive is Moderate; greater than 10 is Gentle. High fog risk applies below 5 only.
questions.explanation: Smaller spacing = steeper slope and higher fog risk per threshold <5.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to interpolate elevation between two contours.
questions.context: Original: identify bounding contours, measure fractional distance, apply linear fraction times interval.

items.label: Identify lower and upper contour elevations

questions.explanation: Identify bounds, measure fraction, scale by interval, add to lower.

questions.prompt: Interpolate the elevation for each described position.
questions.context: Interval 20 m. Linear.

questions.prompt: On the schematic zone diagram, select the zone with the steepest slope (smallest contour spacing).
questions.context: Schematic rectangles: Zone A spacing 8, Zone B spacing 4, Zone C spacing 15, Zone D spacing 6. All elevations labeled in text.

diagram.title: Fog Island Schematic Zones
diagram.description: Four non-overlapping rectangles representing contour spacing zones. Not actual isolines.

questions.explanation: Smallest spacing 4 in Zone B means steepest slope.

questions.prompt: Fog threshold rule: high fog if spacing < 5 units. Which zone triggers high fog under this toy rule?
questions.context: Original invented toy-game threshold for this Fog Island only (not real outdoor advice): high fog if spacing < 5 units. Slope calculations assume same vertical interval and same horizontal units on a fixed linear profile.
questions.explanation: Rule is <5, so 4 triggers high fog. 5 does not (exclusive).

questions.prompt: Relative slope is inversely related to horizontal contour spacing. If spacing doubles, slope roughly...
questions.context: Original approximate on fixed linear profile: slope ~ vertical interval / horizontal spacing (same units). Doubling spacing halves slope. Toy model only.
questions.explanation: Slope proportional to 1/spacing under the fixed linear profile assumption, so doubling spacing halves slope.

questions.prompt: Connect zones to their fog risk level. Connect ALL that match the rule.
questions.context: High risk if spacing <5; medium 5-10 inclusive; low >10.
questions.explanation: Spacing 3 and 4 <5 → high; 8 medium; 12 low. All valid links included.

sources.label: Original fictional Fog Island contour navigation toy model
USGS topographic mapping: contours connect equal elevation points; interval is elevation difference between adjacent contours

note: Original toy model. Schematic rect zones not real maps. Contour basics paraphrased from public USGS resources. No real outdoor or navigation advice. Graphs list every valid link; matches reuse targets only when semantically identical by rule.

title: Spooky Movies, Real Places
description: Find the Massachusetts cemetery outside Salem, the Canadian town playing Maine, and Oregon and Pennsylvania places behind familiar spooky films. Eight discoveries connect screen memories to real geography.

questions.prompt: Allison’s grand house in Hocus Pocus has a real exterior. Which place belongs on the map?
questions.context: Think of the building shown from outside, not every room seen in the film.
questions.explanation: Destination Salem identifies Ropes Mansion in Salem as the exterior of Allison’s house. That pins a specific screen image to a real building without treating its interiors as the film’s interiors.

questions.prompt: The daytime cemetery scene takes the production beyond Salem. Where does that pin move?
questions.context: In Hocus Pocus, Max meets unfriendly classmates in a cemetery by daylight. Destination Salem distinguishes this filming site from its Salem locations.

options.label: To Old Burial Hill in nearby Marblehead, Massachusetts
To Ropes Mansion’s grounds in Salem
To Old Burial Hill in Port Hope, Ontario

questions.explanation: The daylight cemetery footage was made at Old Burial Hill in Marblehead. It is a nearby Massachusetts location, but a different town from Salem.

questions.prompt: Which Salem location supplied the opening village scenes rather than Allison’s house or the cemetery?
questions.context: Follow the film back to its opening, before the modern-day story.
questions.explanation: Pioneer Village supplied the opening scenes. Together with the mansion and Marblehead cemetery, it shows how separate real locations contribute different pieces of the screen setting.

questions.prompt: Derry, Maine is the screen address in IT. Where did Port Hope’s part of that screen town actually stand?
questions.context: The municipality’s film guide covers the IT films and identifies Port Hope as the real filming town behind these Derry locations.
questions.explanation: Port Hope is in Ontario, Canada. Its streets doubled for fictional Derry, Maine; the fictional address does not move the filming town across the international border.

questions.prompt: One Port Hope building can play more than one part. Match these real spaces to their screen roles.
questions.context: Use the municipality’s IT location guide: the building, its lobby and a separate civic building have distinct roles. These are filming relationships, not claims that the fictional businesses exist.

right.label: Arcade used by the Losers’ Club

questions.explanation: The Capitol supplied the movie theatre, while its lobby supplied the arcade. The Visitors Centre doubled as the Chamber of Commerce. A screen neighbourhood can therefore split one real building into two destinations and give another building a new identity.

questions.prompt: The Halloweentown Recreational Center leads to an actual auditorium. Which location is it?
questions.context: A Columbia County Museum notice for the October 17–18, 2026 event identifies the auditorium used in the movie. Here it is evidence of past filming, not an invitation to that now-past event.

options.label: John Gumm Building — St. Helens, Oregon

questions.explanation: The county notice identifies the John Gumm Building auditorium in St. Helens, Oregon, as the Halloweentown Recreational Center. The pin is in the Oregon city, not at a mountain suggested by its name.

questions.prompt: Stay in Oregon, but leave St. Helens for a mountain setting. Which real-place/screen-role pair fits Timberline?
questions.context: Combine the lodge’s own history with its account of The Shining. The question concerns documented exterior footage.

options.label: South slope of Mount Hood — exterior views establishing the fictional Overlook Hotel
Mount Hood — every interior room and corridor of the Overlook
St. Helens — the Halloweentown Recreational Center auditorium
Mount Hood — the daytime cemetery in Hocus Pocus

questions.explanation: Timberline stands on Mount Hood’s south slope in Oregon. Its official film account identifies exterior shots used for the fictional Overlook. That joins a real mountain location to a screen hotel without assigning the interior sets to it.

questions.prompt: The theatre escape in the 1958 Blob was filmed inside and outside a real cinema. Which map pin finds it?
questions.context: The venue’s own 2022 press release describes the filming. Its festival dates and offers are historical, not current travel arrangements.

options.label: John Gumm auditorium — St. Helens, Oregon

questions.explanation: The Colonial Theatre in Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, supplied both inside and outside footage for the scene. Unlike a location used only for an exterior establishing view, this cinema’s connection crosses its own front doors.

title: Strange Landscapes, Real Explanations
description: Follow text-only Halloween field cards through Kentucky limestone, Idaho lava, Utah rock spires, Florida mangroves and New Brunswick coastal weather. Discover why similar eerie moods can come from different places and processes.

sections.title: Compare the Field Cards
sections.description: Coastal contrasts and a final return to the shapes left in rock.

sources.label: NPS: How Mammoth Cave Formed
NPS: Hoodoos at Bryce Canyon
NPS: Craters of the Moon geology for students
NPS: Everglades mangrove ecosystem
Parks Canada: Fundy National Park weather zones
Original fictional Halloween postcard sorting premise

note: Original text descriptions of real North American landscapes, framed as fictional Halloween field cards. No photographs, live map, current weather, access advice or evidence of haunting is supplied. Park references support the physical-geography explanations.

questions.prompt: A Kentucky hallway runs through limestone underground. What process can connect rainwater in the soil with a growing passage below?
questions.context: Text-only field card: Mammoth Cave. Rainwater enters small cracks in the limestone below the soil; the passage is far older than the fictional visitor who calls it a vanishing hallway.
questions.explanation: Mammoth Cave is a solution cave: water enlarged passages by dissolving limestone.

options.label: A single earthquake opening a permanent hallway
Molten rock draining from a cooled crust

questions.prompt: A hollow passage also appears in Idaho lava. Which formation story belongs to this tube rather than Mammoth Cave?
questions.context: Text-only field card: Craters of the Moon. The tunnel sits within an old lava flow, while Mammoth Cave is a passage in limestone. The two underground spaces need not share an origin.
questions.explanation: A lava tube inherits a roof from a cooling flow; Mammoth's cited passage mechanism is dissolution in limestone.

options.label: A hardened lava roof over a drained flow
A coastal current flooding a cave

questions.prompt: Arrange four text sketches as a rock wall becomes a freestanding hoodoo.
questions.context: At Bryce Canyon, weathering and erosion remove material over time. For this simplified sequence, the sketches show successive losses of rock, with no rebuilding. These are text sketches, not a forecast for any individual rock.
questions.explanation: The NPS process diagram moves from plateau to walls to windows to separate hoodoos.

items.label: Cracks divide the plateau into walls
A window opens through a wall

questions.prompt: A crack fills with water, then the high plateau freezes overnight. Which change can help split the rock?
questions.context: Text-only field card: Bryce Canyon. The crack is narrow, and the trapped water cools below its freezing point. Select the mechanism rather than treating the rock shape as a supernatural footprint.
questions.explanation: Ice wedging matters at Bryce: water expands when it freezes and can force cracks apart. Rain also contributes to weathering there, but this card asks about the freeze event.

options.label: Water expands as it freezes and presses against the crack
Freezing water shrinks, sealing the sides together
A cooled lava roof drains from the crack

questions.prompt: Red mangroves stand on stilt-like roots near the tip of Florida. Which water setting belongs to this coastal landscape?
questions.context: Text-only field card: Everglades National Park. The trees occupy coastal channels and winding rivers. Choose the water relationship that explains why this is an estuarine setting.
questions.explanation: The mangrove setting is an estuary influenced by both freshwater and tides.

options.label: Freshwater and saltwater meet near the coast
Only glacial meltwater reaches the roots
The trees grow inside dry lava tubes

questions.prompt: Two fictional Fundy field cards describe different patterns. Which pairing fits the park’s general coast–interior contrast?
questions.context: Card A: cooler summer conditions, frequent fog and milder winters. Card B: warmer summer conditions and typically more winter snow. These summarize climate patterns, not today’s weather or conditions on a particular trail.
questions.explanation: Parks Canada describes a cooler, often foggy coastal zone with milder winters and an inland zone that is warmer in summer and generally snowier in winter. One park can contain both patterns.

options.label: A is coastal; B is inland
A is inland; B is coastal
The differences prove the two cards cannot describe the same park

questions.prompt: Which comparative field notes survive a check across all five places?
questions.context: An editor is joining the five text-only field cards into a North American landscape display. For each pair, choose the comparison supported by the specific places you have explored. A shared eerie appearance does not establish the same formation story.
questions.explanation: The five-place comparison separates appearance, process and setting: Mammoth and Craters have different cave origins, water changes rock in more than one way at Mammoth and Bryce, and the Everglades and Fundy illustrate different coastal relationships. Coast and cave are useful labels, but they do not make every place alike.

cells.label: Mammoth Cave and Craters of the Moon both contain hollow passages.

options.label: Their similar hollow form can result from different rock histories: dissolution and a drained lava flow.
Once both are called caves, the same formation process explains them.

cells.label: Compare Bryce’s rock spires with Mammoth’s limestone passages.

options.label: Water must act in exactly the same way wherever it changes rock.
Water can change rock through different processes, including freezing in cracks and dissolving limestone.

cells.label: Compare the Florida mangrove card with the New Brunswick Fundy cards.

options.label: Both are coastal settings, but one describes a mixed-water habitat and the other a coast–interior climate contrast.
Their coastal setting is enough to give them the same vegetation and climate.

questions.prompt: At Craters of the Moon, why can rock retain a hollow shaped like a tree trunk after the tree is gone?
questions.context: Final text-only field card: a trunk-shaped mold appears in hardened volcanic rock. Pick the formation story that can preserve an outline while removing the original wood.
questions.explanation: NPS describes trees surrounded by hot lava: rock hardened around the trunks, then the wood burned away, leaving molds. The eerie absence has a physical history, rather than being evidence of a vanished ghost forest.

options.label: Lava hardens around a trunk, and the heat burns the wood away
A living tree grows by pushing a trunk-shaped hole through cold solid lava
Rain dissolves wood into limestone and turns that limestone into lava
